findings.suggestion: Kept at blocker deliberately, because what survives the mitigation is a real question for whoever accepted the original trade rather than a settled one. Takedown is still immediate, unmoderated and irreversible - there is no unblock path and updateExpiry answers 409 for a non-ACTIVE link (LinkService.java:169) - so a wrongly-blocked link stays dead, and the P7D gate raises the cost of the attack to seven days of patience per cohort of minted accounts rather than removing it. What a human should confirm: (a) P7D is the intended production value and is not lowered in any deployed profile, and (b) 'an aged account may permanently disable any link whose code it has seen' is the accepted posture. If both hold, close this with no code change. Do not close it as simply wrong: the lens's underlying reasoning - that free accounts change the economics of every per-account limit in the service - is sound, survives the fix, and is carried in top_risks.
findings.summary: The only blocker, and it needs a human for adjudication rather than because the code is unguarded. The security lens reports the abuse-report takedown as gated on nothing but holding an account and knowing a code, now that self-service sign-up makes accounts free. I checked the reviewed tree and the premise is superseded: AbuseReportService.mayTakeDown implements exactly the eligibility rule the lens asks for as its own option (b) - the reporter must pre-date the link, or have existed for app.abuse.min-reporter-age (default P7D, AppProperties.java:227) - the report row is saved before the filter is applied, so the 202-for-everything non-oracle property the lens wanted preserved does hold, and both directions are pinned by AbuseReportReporterAgeTest.anAccountYoungerThanTheMinimumCannotTakeDownALinkItDidNotPreDate and anAccountOlderThanTheMinimumCanTakeDownALinkItDidNotPreDate, plus SignUpIsolationTest for the pre-dating limb. Commit 4c9d74b is titled 'author-tests: pin the abuse-report eligibility rule SEC-1 asks for' and the implementation landed in f419f62, both before this review ran, so this id is a carried-forward concern that was already actioned and re-raised against code that contains the fix.

findings.suggestion: Both lenses independently proposed the same fix, which is a good sign it is the right one: a Semaphore around PasswordHasher.hash/matches sized from the heap or the core count, failing to 503 service_unavailable - the status the create path already uses to shed load. Note the dependency on API-1: without a fallback handler that 503 currently leaves as Boot's default 500 body. The cheaper alternative security names - making SIGN_UP the one bucket that fails closed - is defensible precisely because refusing a sign-up costs a caller a retry rather than a click. Sign-in already carried this exposure and predates the change, but sign-up adds a second entry point on the same key, so fixing it now is better than inheriting it twice. Pin whichever is chosen with a test in AnonymousCreateDegradationTest's style driving sign-up with Redis stopped, and assert the deployed -Xmx against threads x 16 MiB.
findings.summary: Two lenses converged independently on this from opposite directions, which makes it the strongest evidence in the review and the thing to read first after the blocker. Security arrived from 'sign-up is the one unauthenticated write with no other Redis dependency to stop it when the fail-open limiter stops metering'; performance arrived from 'nothing bounds the number of concurrent Argon2id hashes at 16 MiB apiece against Tomcat's default 200 threads'. They are the same defect: unauthenticated POST /api/v1/customers runs a 16 MiB, ~25 ms memory-hard hash with no concurrency bound, and its only meter fails open on any Redis RuntimeException, so during a Redis outage the endpoint is entirely unmetered - on the JVM that also serves the redirect path the requirement says must never be what degrades, and a Redis outage is exactly when the click path is leaning hardest on that JVM. Neither lens saw the other's report; that independent arrival raises my confidence above what either carries alone. POST /api/v1/public/links is not exposed the same way because invalidateBeforeIssuing throws 503 during an outage.

findings.suggestion: Hash outside the transaction: make signUp() non-transactional, compute the hash, then call a small @Transactional insert on a separate bean so the proxy applies. Size the pool explicitly either way - that is the single change that most reduces the blast radius of this, PERF-6 and any future slow call inside a transaction. The lens flags its own assumption honestly (it did not observe Hibernate's acquisition timing with DEBUG on the pool), so confirm before/after by counting pg_stat_activity rows with state='idle in transaction' during a sign-up burst.
findings.summary: signUp() is @Transactional and computes the Argon2id hash (~25 ms, m=16384 KiB) as the first thing inside the transaction, before any statement is issued. With Hikari's default autoCommit=true, Hibernate acquires the JDBC connection at transaction begin rather than at first statement, so a pool connection sits idle-in-transaction for the whole hash. application.yml sets no maximum-pool-size, so the pool is the default 10 and is shared with the redirect cache-miss path - the endpoint that starves is the click path's PostgreSQL fallback. Read this alongside SEC-2: same endpoint, same hash, different failure mode (connection holding versus unbounded concurrency), and a reviewer should fix them in one sitting. The unsized Hikari pool is the shared background condition under this, PERF-6 and the degradation story generally.

findings.suggestion: Add `SET lock_timeout = '3s';` at the top of the migration so it fails fast and is retried rather than head-of-line blocking reads, and run it in a low-traffic window. One line, no behaviour change, and it converts an unbounded stall into a failed migration somebody retries - the highest value-to-effort fix among the majors. Confirm by checking pg_locks for the granted/waiting chain on links while it applies in staging. PERF-8 raises the same class of concern for V3's index build on customers at nit severity.
findings.summary: ALTER TABLE links ALTER COLUMN customer_id DROP NOT NULL is catalog-only and instant, but takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on links - the table the redirect path reads on every cache miss. With no lock_timeout, the ALTER queues behind any in-flight query on links and, while it waits, every later query on links queues behind it, turning a millisecond of DDL into a stall of the hot path for as long as the longest running query, during a deploy, with Flyway blocking startup behind it. This is the one major whose window is deploy day rather than steady state, so it wants a decision before the release rather than after.

findings.suggestion: Add an @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) - or at minimum DataAccessException - that logs and returns 503 service_unavailable in the ApiError shape for the create paths, so the documented degradation contract holds for the dependency that fails most often. If letting 500 escape is genuinely intended, the spec must document a 500 and its body instead. Note the lens executed nothing, so the Boot default body shape is read from framework behaviour rather than observed.
findings.summary: No fallback exception handler. Only ApiException and four Spring binding exceptions are mapped, so anything else - a PostgreSQL outage or a Redis-backed CacheManager failure surfacing as DataAccessException on either create path - propagates to Boot's BasicErrorController and answers 500 with {timestamp,status,error,path}. openapi.yaml lines 717-730 and 570-584 document 503 service_unavailable as the answer when a create-path dependency is unavailable, and lines 121-138 say every non-2xx body has the ApiError shape with a closed catalogue containing no 500. Only two dependency failures are actually translated today. Worth noting for scheduling: SEC-2's recommended fix returns 503 for shed load, so it lands on this gap - fix this first and the shed-load path gets the documented envelope for free. The security lens also records this same missing-handler gap as a pre-existing entry in docs/TODO.md, so it is a known hole being reconfirmed rather than a new discovery.

findings.suggestion: The documentation half is done; what remains is that the behaviour is not configurable at all. Add an explicit app.trusted-proxy-hops or trusted-CIDR property defaulting to getRemoteAddr() so behaviour is unchanged where the header cannot be trusted, and consulting the rightmost untrusted X-Forwarded-For entry where it can. Not trusting an unconfigured header remains the correct default and should stay. Severity kept at major because the confidence-limiting fact is unchanged: whether the proxy preserves the source address is a deployment fact this repository cannot show, and if it does not, several mitigations elsewhere in this review are weaker than their authors believed.
findings.summary: Both new unauthenticated endpoints key their bucket on HttpServletRequest.getRemoteAddr() and nothing sets server.forward-headers-strategy, so behind an edge proxy that does not preserve the source address, ANONYMOUS_CREATE's 30/min and SIGN_UP's 60/min are global ceilings shared by the whole internet rather than per-caller limits - a trivial DoS on both new features, and the quiet premise under three other findings (SEC-7's oracle, SEC-2's Argon2 vector, SEC-4's storage burn) that all name these buckets as their mitigation. One correction to the report: it states docs/RUNBOOK.md contains no mention of proxies or forwarded headers, so the mitigation the design named does not exist. That was true of the tree the security lens read (commit 1898522) but is not true at HEAD - the docs node landed afterwards in 217c1d6, and RUNBOOK.md line 144 now carries exactly that row, naming the global-ceiling consequence, the reason X-Forwarded-For is not trusted, and the instruction to fix it by preserving the source address rather than raising limits.

findings.suggestion: Add "error" to AliasPolicy.RESERVED_CODES. The spec needs no change - it delegates the list to this constant (openapi.yaml lines 1308-1311), which is exactly why the omission is invisible to the route gate. Add a test asserting the alias is refused, since nothing currently would catch a re-deletion. See API-5 for why the surrounding dotted entries make this omission easy to miss.
findings.summary: 'error' is missing from RESERVED_CODES, so POST /api/v1/links {"alias":"error"} answers 201 and mints a code that can never redirect: Boot maps BasicErrorController at /error and a literal PathPattern outranks the /{code} variable pattern, so GET /error answers 500 with Boot's error body rather than the documented 302 - on the one path openapi.yaml line 999 says never returns 5xx. I confirmed the omission directly against the source: the set runs api, actuator, health, info, metrics, prometheus, admin, login, logout, signin, sessions, links, static, assets, docs, status, abuse, support, help, terms, privacy, www and six dotted entries, with no 'error'. Best value-to-effort item in the whole review after PERF-3's one-liner.

findings.suggestion: Inspect the violated constraint (ConstraintViolationException#getConstraintName, or the SQLState for ux_customers_lower_email and ux_customers_email) and translate only those two, rethrowing anything else so it surfaces as a 500 with a stack trace where an operator will see it. The 409's wire behaviour for the case AC6 names is unchanged, so no test should need editing.
findings.summary: Every DataIntegrityViolationException from the sign-up insert is translated to 409 account_unavailable, not just a violation of the lower(email) unique index. Any other integrity fault on this table - a future NOT NULL or FK, or an email that passes @Size(max=320) but overflows a column narrowed in some environment - is reported to the caller as 'that account name is taken' and to the operator as a routine INFO line. A genuine schema fault would be invisible, and the misreport also feeds SEC-7's oracle with false positives. Note the cleanliness lens read the same catch and judged it 'narrow and explained'; the two are not in conflict - it is narrow by exception type and broad by cause, which is precisely the failure mode.

findings.suggestion: Enforce it rather than document it: ALTER TABLE threat_denylist ADD CONSTRAINT ck_threat_denylist_host_canonical CHECK (host = lower(host) AND host NOT LIKE '%.'), so a non-canonical row fails the migration that adds it rather than the block that depends on it. Making the lookup lower(host) with a functional index is cheaper but does not catch the trailing-dot case.
findings.summary: The equivalent-form fix is applied to the query side only. existsByHost is an exact equality match against threat_denylist.host as stored, and nothing enforces stored rows are canonical - V1's schema comment says 'Stored lower-cased' but there is no CHECK constraint, no trigger and no normalisation on insert. A future migration adding 'Malware.Example.COM' or a trailing-dot form would produce a denylist row that silently matches nothing, which is the same class of failure this change exists to close, on the other side of the comparison. Today's two seeded rows are canonical, so nothing fails now. Distinct from TEST-2 despite sharing this file: that one is a missing test for the fail-closed branch, this one is a missing constraint on the data.

findings.suggestion: Add explicit CIDR checks alongside the existing predicates for at least 100.64.0.0/10 and 240.0.0.0/4; the byte-array comparison is the same shape as the fc00::/7 check two lines below. Extend HostEvasionRefusalTest with one case per range so the list cannot silently shrink - and note TEST-3 asks for the mirror-image assertion, that an ordinary public address literal is still shortenable, which is the guard against over-correcting this into refusing legitimate IP targets. Do both together.
findings.summary: isInternalAddress covers loopback, any-local, link-local, site-local, multicast and IPv6 fc00::/7, but not 100.64.0.0/10 (carrier-grade NAT, where Alibaba Cloud's metadata service lives at 100.100.100.200), 192.0.0.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, 240.0.0.0/4 or 255.255.255.255 - none covered by any InetAddress predicate. This is a coverage axis rather than the spelling axis the change was about, and HostNormalizer now guarantees these arrive as canonical dotted quads, so the gap is one predicate wide. Impact is bounded by there being no server-side fetch anywhere in the service, so the exposure is what a clicking browser inside a network reaches, not what this service reaches.

findings.suggestion: Log the client address at INFO alongside the code in createAnonymous, matching what the authenticated path already does with the customer id (LinkService.java:107), and add the address or MDC request id to the sign-up refusal line - the email is rightly absent there, something joinable is not. This is a retention and privacy decision as well as a security one: make it deliberately and note the retention period in docs/RUNBOOK.md. A hash of the address with a rotating salt is a reasonable middle position if raw addresses are unwanted.
findings.summary: Two lenses independently found the new unauthenticated write paths log nothing joinable, at two different sites, with the same one-line fix - security at anonymous creation (LinkService.java:141, where the log line carries only the generated code and the row carries no creator by construction) and cleanliness at the duplicate sign-up refusal (SignUpService.java:68, where a spike of 409s cannot be attributed to one caller versus many). Both sites already have the client address in hand two frames up the stack for the rate-limit key. When an anonymous link turns out to be a phishing redirect there is nothing to pivot on: no way to find the same creator's other links, no way to block the source, no evidence for a report. Kept at the higher of the two severities. This is also the finding that makes SEC-4's storage-burn observable, so it is worth more than its severity suggests.

findings.suggestion: Decide before ship rather than after the table is large. A scheduled hard delete of links where customer_id IS NULL AND expires_at < now() - grace is safe precisely because nobody owns them and no API can reference them after expiry - but note reissuing their codes is explicitly forbidden, so a reaper needs a tombstone and the namespace remains monotonic either way. At minimum expose a gauge for the count of unowned rows plus the ANONYMOUS_CREATE 429 rate, so growth is observable before it is a capacity incident, which the requirement's operability criterion asks for anyway.
findings.summary: Security and performance converged on this independently: anonymous rows have no owner, cannot be deleted by anyone (AnonymousLinkInvisibilityTest confirms DELETE answers 404), and are never reclaimed - V1's model is soft-delete-only, expiry is derived at read time rather than swept, and this change adds no purge job. Expired anonymous rows accumulate permanently in links and in ix_links_owner_listing, each carrying up to 2048 bytes of attacker-chosen long_url, and each holding its (domain, code) namespace slot forever. The performance lens puts it best on the bound: the growth rate is set by attacker choice rather than by anything in this service, since the only ceiling is a per-IP bucket that SEC-3 argues may be global and that fails open when Redis is unreachable. The requirement's non-functional criterion is explicit that an unauthenticated write endpoint must not become an unmetered storage-burn vector.

findings.suggestion: Extract `private URI admittedTarget(String longUrl)` performing the parse, requireShortenable and requirePermittedTarget, and call it from both. The methods stay separate, which the design justifies; only the rule set is shared. Partial mitigation already exists in the suite - theAnonymousPathAcceptsNoTargetTheAuthenticatedPathRefuses compares the two paths - so a divergence would be caught, though as a status-code mismatch rather than as anything readable (see TEST-6, which notes that same test is the one silently depending on a production rate-limit default).
findings.summary: createAnonymous re-types the three-line target-admission sequence from create() (parseOrThrow, requireShortenable, requirePermittedTarget). The javadoc promises the two paths must never differ in what they accept (AC12) but nothing mechanical holds them together: a fourth rule added to create() will silently not apply to the anonymous path. Worth reading next to SEC-9, which proposes adding exactly such a rule - the internal-address CIDR checks - which is the concrete way this duplication turns into a security divergence rather than a style complaint.

findings.suggestion: Move invalidateBeforeIssuing outside the transactional boundary (commit, then invalidate, then respond - the 503-on-failure semantics can be preserved in the controller or a wrapper bean), or explicitly size the pool for the slow-Redis case. Sizing the pool is shared with PERF-1 and is the cheaper first move. Confirm by holding Redis at a 1s delay and watching HikariCP pending-connection count.
findings.summary: createAnonymous holds the database transaction open across a Redis round trip: resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(code) runs inside @Transactional after saveAndFlush. Redis timeouts are 1s connect and 1s read, so a brownout parks a pool connection for up to ~2s per request; with the default pool of 10 and an unauthenticated caller supplying the traffic, a slow-but-not-dead Redis converts into pool exhaustion for everything else including the redirect cache-miss path. The pattern mirrors create() exactly and is pre-existing - what is new is that it is reachable without a credential, which is the theme running through most of this review.

findings.suggestion: Make it partial: CREATE INDEX ... WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL, as a separate migration once anonymous volume is known - and note PERF-3's lock_timeout lesson applies to that migration too. Confirm with pg_relation_size on the index and a count of NULL-owner rows after a few weeks.
findings.summary: ix_links_owner_listing (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) now carries anonymous rows for the first time: a btree indexes NULLs, and every anonymous link adds an entry under a leading NULL that no query can ever match, because findOwnedBy and findByDomainAndCodeAndCustomerId are equality-scoped. The migration comment says the index 'never serves an anonymous row', which is true of reads and not of writes - insert cost, index size and vacuum work are all paid. Magnitude depends entirely on anonymous volume, which nobody has measured; at low volume this is invisible. Same underlying cause as SEC-4 (unbounded unowned rows), different cost, so fixing the retention question shrinks this one too.

findings.suggestion: No new machinery and no sweeper needed: a one-off query over links whose long_url host normalises to a denylisted or internal form, reviewed and then blocked through the same markBlocked path abuse reports use, run once as part of the deploy. Whether to run it is a human decision about breaking live links; what should not happen is the question never being asked because A4 closed it in the design. This is the one finding whose window closes at deploy time rather than staying open, so decide it with the release.
findings.summary: requirePermittedTarget and requireShortenable run on the create paths only; nothing re-evaluates an already-issued link. The design states this (A4, 'no retroactive rescan') and it is a defensible scope boundary, but the consequence belongs in front of whoever accepts it: any link minted through the two bypasses this change closes - a denylisted host with a trailing dot, an internal address in numeric form - keeps redirecting for the remainder of its TTL, up to 30 days, while the service refuses to mint the same target. The requirement's goal sentence is 'close the ways a known-dangerous URL can slip past the safety filter', and for already-minted links it is not closed.

findings.suggestion: No code change is right here without the human decision the design already asked for, and it is the same human as SEC-3. Fixing SEC-3 so the bound is genuinely per-caller is what changes the risk, at which point 60 addresses/min/source is a defensible cost for a disclosure AC6 requires. Q2's 400 fallback discloses exactly the same fact and is not an improvement. Note SEC-8 currently feeds this oracle false positives, so fix that regardless.
findings.summary: 409 account_unavailable is an account-existence oracle in a service that otherwise goes to deliberate lengths not to be one - identical 401s for unknown-account and wrong-password, timing-equalised sign-in, no 403, no 410, one fixed 422 message for every host refusal. The security lens is explicit that it is restating an already-adjudicated decision rather than re-litigating it, because the acceptance rested on the SIGN_UP bucket being a meaningful bound and SEC-3 argues that bucket may be global in the target deployment. The two compound: an oracle bounded by a global 60/min is enumerable by anyone willing to spend the whole service's sign-up allowance. Kept at the lens's severity, but a reviewer should treat it as a consequence of SEC-3 rather than an independent decision to remake.

findings.suggestion: Amend openapi.yaml lines 78-82 to drop 999.999.999.999 and 'an empty label' as 422 examples, and say instead that hosts java.net.URI cannot parse are 400 and only canonicalisation failures on a parseable host are 422. No code change. Note the lens executed nothing, so the java.net.URI behaviour is asserted from reading plus the fixtures' agreement, not from an observed run - cheap to confirm with a one-line JShell check before editing a frozen contract.
findings.summary: Out-of-range dotted numeric hosts answer 400 invalid_request, not the 422 url_rejected the spec demands. openapi.yaml lines 78-82 give 999.999.999.999 and 'an empty label' as 422 examples, but java.net.URI returns a null host for those forms on JDK 21, so parseOrThrow rejects them as 400 before HostNormalizer is consulted - exactly as lines 98-101 of the same document say it should. Single-label overflow (http://0x100000000/) does reach HostNormalizer and does answer 422, so only the dotted forms diverge. This is one of two places where the lens concludes the spec is wrong and the code is right; the test branch read it the same way (Fixtures.java:359-365 classes these as unparseable), which is corroboration from a third direction.

findings.suggestion: Change the spec: qualify the ApiError-shape sentence to cover only statuses this document declares, and say explicitly that dispatcher-level 404/405/415 carry Boot's default body. Do this in the same edit as API-3 and API-5, which are also spec-side.
findings.summary: Framework default error bodies leak on undeclared failure paths: 405 on wrong verbs for the two new paths and /{code}, 415 for a non-JSON Content-Type, and 404 for an unmatched path. All return Boot's error JSON rather than ApiError. openapi.yaml line 121 states flatly that every non-2xx response has the ApiError shape while lines 58-61 and 230 deliberately delegate 405 to Spring's dispatcher; both cannot be true. The status codes themselves are right - 405 rather than 401 on the newly exempted paths is documented behaviour and the test lens independently confirms it is asserted - so this is a spec defect, not a code defect. Distinct from API-1 despite the same file and line: that is a missing handler for dependency failures, this is dispatcher-level statuses the spec overclaims about.

findings.suggestion: Add theEmailMaximumLengthIsInclusiveAndAnythingAboveItIsRefused in the shape of the existing password pair: 320 characters signs up with 201 and can then sign in; 321 answers 400 invalid_request with fields.email and leaves storedAccountsNamed empty. Clearest fix in the test set - it has an exact template to copy.
findings.summary: SignUpRequest declares @Size(max = 320) on email and nothing tests either side of it. The password boundaries are pinned twice over, each asserting the fixture really sits on the boundary, so the omission is asymmetric rather than a house convention. An address ceiling that was dropped or set to the wrong number would be found by nothing - and the column width is what it is protecting, which is also the failure SEC-8 says would currently be misreported to the caller as 409 'account name taken'. The two findings meet here: the missing boundary test is what lets the mistranslation stay invisible.

findings.suggestion: Add a DenylistThreatCheckTest against a stub repository that lists nothing: aHostThatCannotBeCanonicalisedIsBlocked asserting verdict(URI.create("http://4294967296/")) == BLOCK with an empty denylist, so the mock cannot be what produces the answer, plus aCanonicalisedHostIsMatchedAgainstTheDenylist asserting the trailing-dot form of a listed row matches while notmalware.example.com does not. The second assertion also gives SEC-6 a place to live once the CHECK constraint exists.
findings.summary: DenylistThreatCheck returns BLOCK when the host cannot be canonicalised, and nothing pins it: the branch is unobservable over HTTP because UrlValidator.requireShortenable refuses the same host with 422 first, and there is no unit test for DenylistThreatCheck anywhere in the suite. Deleting the three lines would fail nothing. The code comment states exactly the property at stake - 'a security property that holds only because they run in a particular order is one reordering away from not holding' - and that property is currently held by no test, so reordering the two checks keeps the suite green. This is defence-in-depth that the contract specified and the implementation honoured; only the test is missing.

findings.suggestion: Add aNonAsciiHostIsCanonicalisedToItsPunycodeForm: assert normalize("bücher.example.com") equals Optional.of("xn--bcher-kva.example.com"), that the result is all-ASCII, that it is idempotent, and that a non-ASCII host IDN.toASCII rejects answers Optional.empty() rather than the input. Unit level only; no HTTP path needed.
findings.summary: The IDN/punycode step of HostNormalizer (step 4 of the frozen contract) has no test at any level. Every other row of the worked table is pinned - trailing dots, case, all four numeric forms, octal, out-of-range, empty labels, IPv6, idempotence, no-label-removal - but no test passes a non-ASCII host, so deleting the IDN.toASCII branch or replacing it with a pass-through leaves the suite green. The javadoc argues the step is unreachable through HTTP and says it exists 'so the guarantee does not depend on that', which is precisely a guarantee nothing checks. Same shape as TEST-2: the deliberate defence-in-depth branches are the ones without tests, which is understandable and is exactly where a later refactor will quietly remove them.

findings.suggestion: Add HostEvasionRefusalTest.aPublicAddressLiteralIsStillShortenable: POST a target with host 93.184.216.34, assert 201, assert longUrl comes back byte-identical, and assert a click sends Location to the submitted URL. Adding it to LOOKALIKE_URLS_STILL_ACCEPTED also makes the existing lookalike test cover it and makes theAnonymousPathAcceptsNoTargetTheAuthenticatedPathRefuses compare it on both paths.
findings.summary: The accept side of host normalisation is only exercised with registered names: every URL in the suite whose host is numeric is one that must be refused, so no test asserts that an ordinary public address literal such as https://93.184.216.34/x is still shortenable. An implementation that failed closed on any host the normaliser rewrote, or treated every IPv4 candidate as internal, would pass all seventeen AC1/AC2 behaviours and silently stop customers shortening IP-literal targets - the over-refusal failure that impact.json and the design both nominate as the most dangerous one here. This is the guard rail for SEC-9's proposed CIDR additions, which are exactly the kind of change that could over-refuse; add this test before making that change.

findings.suggestion: Pin the assumption on the class: @SpringBootTest(properties = Fixtures.ANONYMOUS_CREATE_LIMIT_KEY + "=1000"), with a javadoc line saying the class needs the limit not to be reached and that throttling is AnonymousCreateRateLimitTest's subject. Two-line fix that removes a coupling between a production default and an unrelated test's failure mode.
findings.summary: theAnonymousPathAcceptsNoTargetTheAuthenticatedPathRefuses issues 25 anonymous creates in one method, and the bucket is charged before validation so all 25 spend a token. The class declares no properties, so it runs against the production default of 30: five requests of headroom, undeclared. The design explicitly invites an operator to lower it ('An operator who wants 10 changes one number'), and adding two fixtures to any of the three lists has the same effect. Every other class depending on a bucket size pins it; this one depends on it silently and would fail as a status-code mismatch between the two paths rather than as anything readable - which matters because this is the same test CLEAN-1 relies on to catch a divergence between the create paths.

findings.suggestion: Assert that at least one of the three attempts answered 503, keeping the existing per-response envelope assertions. If a run shows creation legitimately survives, say so in the javadoc rather than leaving a reader to infer the branch was checked. Note SEC-2 proposes a new degradation test in this same class's style for sign-up; whoever writes that should decide the unconditional-assertion question once for both.
findings.summary: AC15's refusal half is asserted only conditionally, so it may never be exercised: every claim about the 503 envelope is guarded behind allMatch(201 || 503) then filters, so an implementation whose anonymous create survives the Redis outage passes this class with the service_unavailable code, the catalogue message and the 'refused with the existing error response' sentence of AC15 never checked. Per the design the pre-issue cache invalidation makes the 503 deterministic when the shared tier is paused, so the tolerance is wider than the implementation needs. The lens is careful to note this is the existing house pattern (DegradedDependencyTest is written identically), so it is a consistency judgement rather than a defect introduced here - which also means fixing it is optional but fixing the pattern is worth a decision.

findings.suggestion: Sleep a quarter of the TTL rather than half, or compute the wait from link.expiresAt() rather than the constant (wait until halfway between Instant.now() and expiresAt), so the margin shrinks with the round trip instead of being fixed. Keep the halfWay guard assertion either way.
findings.summary: anAnonymousLinkRedirectsUntilItsExpiryPasses runs against a 3-second TTL, sleeps half of it, and needs the second click to complete before expiry - two HTTP round trips plus first-call warm-up inside ~1.5s. It fails loudly rather than silently, since assertTrue(halfWay.isBefore(link.expiresAt())) exists precisely to name the wall clock as the cause, but on a loaded CI box this is the shape of test that gets muted, and a muted expiry test takes AC10 with it. Nothing else in the class has the problem - the other methods wait past expiry rather than racing it. Worth weighing against the triage record showing this suite is already sensitive to harness resource limits.

findings.suggestion: No test change. Before AC3 is signed, show a human the recorded failing run against the pre-change commit, or record an explicit statement that the ordering was not observed. Cheap to produce now by checking out the pre-change commit and running the two named methods; much harder to reconstruct later.
findings.summary: AC3 has two halves and only one is met inside the repository. The tests that would have failed against pre-change code exist and are retained, and the lens is confident they would genuinely have failed. But AC3 also requires that failure to have been produced and visible before the fix, and plan.json T1 lists 'run log entry recording the failing run against pre-change code' as a deliverable: nothing under artifacts/ records a red run, and the pipeline's verify node runs after join, i.e. only ever against fixed code. The test javadoc concedes the evidence has to come from outside the suite. This is the one finding no code change can close, and it generalises - see top_risks, where the absence of any executed verification in this entire review is the larger version of the same gap.

findings.suggestion: Document the actuator surface and its authentication posture in the spec's surfaces table, or scope it to a management port. No code change is needed for contract conformance - but if the release gate cares about unauthenticated surfaces, this one has not actually been security-reviewed by anybody in this run.
findings.summary: Undocumented surface: /actuator/health, /info, /metrics and /prometheus are exposed and sit outside the session filter, which is registered only for /api/v1/* (WebConfig.java:28,36). The spec's 'Three surfaces' table presents its list as exhaustive and never mentions actuator. Pre-existing rather than introduced here, but undocumented behaviour becomes a de facto contract as soon as a caller depends on it. Promoting this above the other nits because the security lens listed the same actuator exposure in its not_examined - so it is simultaneously a contract nit and an acknowledged hole in the security review, and a reviewer should know the two are the same surface.

findings.suggestion: Add `private String shortUrl(LinkEntity link)` and use it from both response builders. Do it with CLEAN-1.
findings.summary: The short URL is assembled as baseUrl + "/" + link.getCode() in two places (toResponse and createAnonymous). Small, but it is the kind of duplication that drifts the day baseUrl gains a trailing-slash rule or a path prefix. Same file and the same root cause as CLEAN-1 - the anonymous path was written by copying the authenticated one - so both extractions are one sitting's work.

findings.suggestion: Have radixOf return the digit offset alongside the radix (a small private record, or a single parsePart returning the value or -1), so the prefix rule exists in exactly one place. Low priority, but this is the file where a future editor is most likely to introduce a security-relevant mistake, which is an argument for making it read cleanly.
findings.summary: The radix rules are encoded twice: radixOf decides the base from the 0x/leading-zero prefix, and valueOf re-derives both the radix and the prefix length in a switch. Two encodings of the same rule in one file, and the second only makes sense if you have read the first. Worth noting the surrounding context - the security lens probed this same parser hard for radix confusion, integer overflow and Unicode-digit tricks and found nothing wrong - so this is a maintainability observation about correct code, not a hint of a latent bug.

findings.suggestion: Implement Persistable<UUID> with a transient isNew flag, or inject EntityManager and call persist() directly. Confirm with Hibernate SQL logging on a single sign-up: two statements today, one after. Fix service-wide or not at all - doing it only for sign-up would make the pattern inconsistent for no real gain.
findings.summary: CustomerEntity has an application-assigned UUID id, no @Version and does not implement Persistable, so Spring Data's isNew() sees a non-null id and routes saveAndFlush through merge() - Hibernate issues a SELECT by primary key before every INSERT. One wasted round trip per sign-up. The same is true of every link insert, so this is a pre-existing house pattern rather than something this change introduced; noting it mainly because it lengthens the transaction PERF-1 wants shortened.

findings.suggestion: If it is ever worth touching: build the candidate list and ask once (existsByHostIn(candidates)), and skip the parent walk entirely when the canonical host is a dotted quad. The second half is the one with an actual correctness flavour - walking parents of an IP address is meaningless by construction - so it is worth a comment even if the query count is left alone.
findings.summary: isListed issues one existsByHost query per parent label inside the create transaction - four to six round trips for an ordinary hostname. Newly, HostNormalizer canonicalises numeric hosts to dotted quads, so an IP target now walks 127.0.0.1 -> 0.0.1 -> 0.1 -> 1: four queries whose answers cannot be meaningful, on both create paths. Each is a unique-index hit on a tiny table, so the cost is round trips rather than work, and create is not the hot path. The lens's own verdict is that this is a rounding error at any plausible load; carried as a nit for completeness.

findings.suggestion: Note the expected build time against the production row count in the approval for this protected-path migration. If customers is ever large, split it into a non-transactional Flyway migration using CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Also note the security lens's separate point that the duplicate-check query this migration's comment requires must be run by a human against each environment before it applies - that is a deploy precondition, not a code change.
findings.summary: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY, and Flyway wraps the migration in a transaction so CONCURRENTLY is unavailable without extra configuration) takes a SHARE lock on customers for the duration of the build, blocking writes - i.e. sign-ups and nothing else, since sign-in only reads. Harmless at the current table size; worth knowing it scales with the customer count, which self-service sign-up is precisely the feature that makes grow. Same family as PERF-3 but far smaller blast radius, since it blocks the new endpoint rather than the click path.

findings.suggestion: Add a comment noting that dotted names are refused by the pattern, so the list only has to cover single-segment route names - or drop the dotted entries. Either way, do it in the same edit as API-4 so the list and its rationale end up consistent.
findings.summary: Six RESERVED_CODES entries are unreachable: robots.txt, favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, index.html, security.txt and .well-known all contain a dot, and requireAcceptable checks well-formedness against ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}$ before it checks reservation, so those aliases are already refused on the pattern. Harmless in itself, but the spec quotes this list as the authority and a reader will infer it is load-bearing where it is not - which is exactly the misreading that lets API-4's missing 'error' entry go unnoticed. I confirmed both facts against the source in one read: six dotted entries present, 'error' absent.

findings.suggestion: Either map the enum to the hyphenated names or note in the spec that the key segment is the enum name lower-cased. Worth deciding before a dashboard, runbook or ops script starts matching on the key - and note that three lenses independently listed redis/token_bucket.lua as unread, so the key format is not the only thing about these buckets nobody has verified.
findings.summary: Redis bucket key names differ from the spec's names: openapi.yaml pins keys as ratelimit:<bucket>:<key> with hyphenated bucket names (not-found, abuse-report, sign-in, sign-up, anonymous-create), while keyFor derives the segment from the enum constant, producing ratelimit:not_found:, ratelimit:sign_up: and so on. No wire effect, and the load-bearing property - that no bucket can spend another's tokens, so exhausting anonymous-create leaves write untouched (AC14) - holds.

summary: A strong change: the contract is honoured on every documented operation, all sixteen acceptance criteria have behaviour-named tests that would fail if reverted, and the security lens - which probed the new HostNormalizer hard for radix confusion, overflow, over-normalisation and Unicode tricks - found nothing wrong with the part of the diff that is actually about security. Read the merged SEC-2/PERF-2 finding first: security and performance arrived independently at the same defect, an unauthenticated sign-up endpoint running an unbounded, 16 MiB memory-hard hash whose only meter fails open during a Redis outage, on the JVM that also serves the redirect path. The single blocker (SEC-1) should be adjudicated rather than fixed: I verified that the reporter-eligibility rule it asks for is already implemented (app.abuse.min-reporter-age, default P7D) and tested in both directions, so the human's question is narrower than the report implies - whether a seven-day age gate adequately bounds an irreversible takedown that still has no unblock path. Nothing here obviously stops the release, but the release gate should weigh one thing the findings cannot express: not one of the five lenses executed anything - no build, no test run, no query plan, no HTTP request - so every severity above is reasoned from reading source.
top_risks: Nothing was executed by any lens. All five reports independently list this in not_examined: api-contract ('no build, no test run, no HTTP request'), security ('Ran nothing'), test-adequacy ('I did not run the suite... no verify artifact exists for this run'), performance ('No EXPLAIN was run'). The last recorded run in triage.json shows 276 tests with 5 errors, all in WriteRateLimitTest and all from PostgreSQL 'too many clients already' attributed to the harness connection budget rather than the code - so the most recent evidence of the suite passing is both incomplete and pre-join. Every claim in this document about framework behaviour (Boot's default error bodies, /error outranking /{code}, java.net.URI's null host, Hibernate's connection-acquisition timing) is read, not observed.

redis/token_bucket.lua was read by nobody. Three lenses list it explicitly as unexamined. This matters more than any single finding: the rate-limit buckets are the named mitigation for the account-existence oracle (SEC-7), the Argon2 exhaustion vector (SEC-2), the anonymous storage burn (SEC-4), and the abuse-report escalation behind the blocker. The atomicity of the two new buckets, their key expiry, and whether capacity is applied as the Java side expects are all decided in a file no reviewer opened, and the Retry-After semantics under real contention are unverified.

Every new unauthenticated capability was correctly identified as needing a token bucket, and each bucket now carries more weight than one bucket keyed by a possibly-shared address can hold. Even with all findings fixed, four separate risk acceptances rest on the same mechanism, and SEC-3's premise - whether the edge proxy preserves the source address - is a deployment fact this repository cannot settle. If it does not, the buckets are global ceilings and four mitigations are weaker than their authors believed, simultaneously.

Self-service sign-up permanently changes the economics of every per-account limit in the service, not just the one the blocker names. The reporter-age rule closes the abuse-report path, but 'signed-in' is now free for any future per-account budget, and no artifact in this run (clarification.json, design.json, impact.json) weighs that as a general property rather than a single endpoint's problem.

Deployment and resource facts are absent from the repository entirely. There is no Dockerfile, k8s manifest, JVM flag, heap size, thread cap or replica count anywhere, and Hikari's pool is never sized (default 10). Every 'at what load' statement in the performance findings is arithmetic from configured limits rather than measurement, and nobody has run this under load - so the severities reflect cost-when-wrong, not observed behaviour.

Anonymous rows are unbounded and irreversible in a way no single fix fully closes: even with the reaper SEC-4 asks for, reissuing codes is explicitly forbidden, so the (domain, code) namespace grows monotonically with attacker-chosen input. Likewise the abuse-report takedown has no unblock path anywhere in the service, so every takedown - correct or not - is permanent.

AC3's required evidence does not exist in the repository and cannot be produced by any test: the pipeline's verify node runs only after join, i.e. only ever against fixed code, so no red run against pre-change code was ever recorded. The same structural gap makes the AC3 sign-off, the V3 duplicate-email pre-check, and the pre-change ordering claim all things a human must assert from outside the artifacts.

Whole subsystems were reviewed by nobody. JWT issuance and verification (including app.session.private-key-pem defaulting to blank, which generates an ephemeral keypair per replica), the actuator surface that sits outside the session filter, clickCount exactness and the flush job, and dependency/CVE scanning are each listed as unexamined by at least one lens and covered by none. The actuator gap appears as a contract nit (API-6) and as a security not_examined entry, which means it has been noticed twice and reviewed zero times.
